analysis.one_liner: Makes the Bush-era income tax cuts permanent, repeals the estate tax, and indexes investment gains for inflation.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2012 with no cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote or any floor action before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make permanent the income tax rate cuts from 2001 and 2003, including the low tax rates on dividends and capital gains. It would repeal the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax entirely, cut gift tax rates to a flat 35%, and allow a $5 million lifetime gift tax exemption. It would also make the tuition deduction and generous small-business equipment expensing permanent, patch the alternative minimum tax for 2012, and let sellers of assets held more than three years increase their cost basis for inflation before calculating taxable gains.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, households at all income levels would have kept the lower income tax rates permanently, with the largest dollar gains going to high earners through the low dividend and capital gains rates. Families with college costs would keep the tuition deduction. Small businesses would keep the $125,000 equipment expensing allowance. Very wealthy households would gain the most from full estate tax repeal, the cut gift tax rates, and inflation indexing of investment gains.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and large estates, plus small firms

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the individual income tax rates from the 2001 and 2003 tax acts, including reduced rates on dividend and capital gain income.
Repeals the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax for deaths and transfers on or after enactment.
Makes the deduction for tuition and related expenses permanent, and makes the increased small-business expensing allowance ($125,000 deduction, $500,000 phaseout, inflation-adjusted) permanent.
Extends the alternative minimum tax exemption to 2012 and, going forward, adjusts the exemption for inflation so middle-income households are not pulled into the AMT each year.
Allows taxpayers to increase the cost basis of assets held more than three years by inflation before computing gain, reducing tax on long-held investments and property.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on the federal treasury, since the bill contains no offsetting tax increases; the bill's own findings frame this as shrinking the federal tax burden from a projected 21 percent of GDP back toward historical levels. The revenue loss would ultimately be borne by future taxpayers through borrowing or through later spending cuts. The estate tax repeal specifically benefits only estates large enough to owe the tax.

drawbacks.text: Full repeal of the estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax removes a tax paid only by the largest estates, converting a progressive revenue source into an unpaid-for windfall for very wealthy heirs.
The bill includes no revenue offsets: making the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent, repealing the estate tax, and indexing capital gains for inflation all reduce federal revenue, adding to deficits.
The gift tax changes cut rates to a flat 35 percent and set a $5 million lifetime exemption, making it cheaper to transfer very large fortunes during life rather than at death.

Inflation indexing of basis applies to stocks and tangible property held more than three years, a benefit that concentrates among households with large appreciated assets, though it requires written documentation of purchase price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles real middle-class provisions — permanent lower rates, an AMT patch, the tuition deduction, and small-business expensing — with provisions whose benefits flow overwhelmingly to the top of the income distribution: full estate tax repeal, a flat 35 percent gift tax, and inflation indexing of investment gains. All of it is deficit-financed, with no pay-fors, and the bill makes no attempt to separate the broadly popular parts from the estate and gift tax repeals that drew no support beyond the sponsor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and sat there without a markup or floor vote until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on July 26, 2012, during the run-up to the 2012 election and the scheduled expiration of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day and received no further action.
No member of either party cosponsored the bill.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill still in committee, so it never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury avoided an unpaid-for loss of revenue, and large estates remained subject to the estate tax. The bill's sponsor and supporters got no policy change; middle-class taxpayers got the AMT patch and rate decisions through other legislation instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal treasury; large estates still taxed

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 26, 2012 to make the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and repeal the estate tax.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action; no markup was held and no floor vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only sponsor was a Republican and it drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Very wealthy households and large estates
industries.note: The bill repeals the estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax outright and cuts gift tax rates to a flat 35 percent with a $5 million lifetime exemption. These taxes apply only to the largest estates and transfers, so the gain is concentrated at the top while the lost revenue is shared by all taxpayers.

Permanent low rates on dividends and capital gains, plus the new inflation indexing for assets held over three years, reduce taxes on investment income. The benefit scales with the size of the portfolio and the cost shows up as deficit-financed revenue loss.

The bill makes the $125,000 equipment expensing allowance permanent, inflation-adjusted, with a $500,000 phaseout, letting small firms deduct equipment purchases immediately rather than over time. The benefit is not limited to low-income owners, but it does not come at the public's expense in the way the estate provisions do.
